title: Climbing & Balancing
strapline: Wobbles, brave steps and the view from the top — bodies learning what they can do.
intent: Build core strength, grip and whole-body coordination through climbing, hanging and traversing.
Develop balance and body awareness on beams, planks, stepping stones and uneven ground.
Learn to judge risk for themselves — how high, how fast, which foot next — with adults nearby, not in charge.
Grow persistence and courage: the top of the frame is earned, not given.
Use position and height language in real, felt contexts — over, under, across, higher.
Experience the confidence that comes from a body that does what you ask of it.
implementation: Build varied low-level courses — crates, planks, beams, tyres — and change the layout weekly so bodies keep problem-solving.
Spot with hands ready but off: 'I'm here' beats lifting a child to a place their body hasn't earned yet.
Say what you see, not 'be careful': 'That plank wobbles when you step in the middle', 'Your hands are gripping tightly.'
Let children come down the way they got up — climbing down is the harder skill and worth the wait.
Offer graded challenge side by side: a wide beam next to a narrow one, a low crate next to a stack, so every child finds their edge.
Resist tidying the wobble out — uneven, springy, tilting surfaces are the curriculum.
Notice and name the process: 'You tried three ways before your foot found that hold.'
key_questions: Which part of your body is doing the hardest work right now?
How could you get across without touching the ground?
What does the wobbly plank make your arms do?
Where will your foot go next — how do you know?
What can you see from up there that you can't see from down here?
That bit felt tricky — what would make it feel safer for you?

impact.text: The youngest climbers pull up onto low crates and steps, squatting, crawling over and clambering with growing confidence.
Children balance along low beams and planks — first gripping a steadying hand, then arms-out alone.
Children read an obstacle course with their bodies — adjusting stride for gaps, ducking, judging where hands and feet go.
A child sticks at a traverse that beat them yesterday, tries different holds, and beams 'I did it!' from the top.
Height and position talk flows through the play: higher, across, under the plank, the wobbliest one.
Children direct and coach each other across the course — 'hold this bit, now big step' — using talk to keep the challenge going.
Older children explain their route and their thinking — how they got up, why one way was too wobbly, what they'll try next.
By the time they leave us for school, children climb and balance with genuine control, choosing challenges at their own edge and moving with confidence.

enhancements: A 'river' of blue fabric under the beam — the crossing suddenly matters.
Stepping stones spaced by the children themselves — how far apart is still possible?
A springy plank (plank over a tyre) next to a firm one — same walk, different body.
Carry challenges: cross the beam holding a beanbag, then a cup of water, then one in each hand.
Chalk-numbered stones so the route becomes a counting trail.
A pulley and bucket at the top of the frame — a reason to climb up and a job to do there.
Photograph a child mid-climb and revisit it together: 'Tell me what your body was doing here.'

playing_exploring: Children choose their own challenge from the graded options, finding the edge between easy and scary.
New layouts are investigated with hands and feet before words — testing, patting, pressing.
active_learning: Falls and wobbles are met with another go — the crate that defeated them is returned to, sometimes days later.
Deep concentration is visible: tongue out, eyes on feet, the world elsewhere.
creating_thinking: Children invent their own rules and routes — lava floors, one-hand-only crossings, backwards challenges.
They rework the course itself, dragging crates and planks into new problems to solve.
